rv.q: The acting here is dauntless: a monumental testament to domestic agony.
A riveting period portrait - and a heart-rending mirror of forsaken souls in which we may all glimpse our own familial griefs.
Jeremy Herrin’s production is full of pathos and ruined grandeur, with superb performances all round.
The subtle family dynamics are beautifully traced and the ending is magnificent.
Watching these fine actors bring to life a family wrecked by addiction, their love for one another corroded by hatred, is sad but also weirdly uplifting.
By no means is this a perfect production.

The almost three-and-a-half hours of Jeremy Herrin’s production do weigh heavily, as the four members of the tormented Tyrone family, variously addicted to alcohol, drugs and self-delusion, each seek their own oblivion.
Solo confessions are the motor of the play but they gain in intensity with a greater sense of family – of inherited and inescapable dysfunction – than there is here.
Some scenes glitter with dark energy, and are truly tragic.
Cox is decent, but I found his performance diffused by the production.
By turns stern and maudlin, Cox is always watchable, but he’s still not able to prevent long-winded confrontations and confessions from slipping into melodrama.
The show proves to be a pretty good approximation of purgatory - and that’s really not an experience I can in good conscience recommend to anyone.
These are fine performances in a clear-headed production of a major work that finds humour at many points, however dark it is overall.

Its revival will allow both old friends of the play and new audiences to come along to enjoy four vibrant lead performances and a character bit from Louisa Harland, the long-suffering maid from 'the old country'.
O’Neill’s play...in the hands of such a talented cast...it is powerful theatre.
The clarity and directness of Herrin’s production and the way that the cast both speak and listen with absolute intent brings it to vivid life once more.
Jeremy Herrin's slow-aborning if properly sorrowful production confirms a sense confirmed by experience that this text really does belong to Mary.
Overall, however, his production doesn’t fully sustain the tricky balancing act.
Brian Cox captures this gruff and friendless ogre very well, but the play is an unbearable torment.
This gripping production of Long Day’s Journey Into Night lingers long after the curtain comes down.
This is a fine production of Long Day’s Journey Into Night, and Herrin’s direction keeps it feeling relatively fresh.
A long but rewarding night in the theatre.
Clarkson is magnificent and yet I left underwhelmed.
The weight of talent behind this new production is undeniable – but the show is fundamentally weighed down by an unwieldy script packed with laboured metaphors worn thin by relentless repetition.

cn.t: Cox and Clarkson deliver powerful performances in this bleak, exhausting marathon, though critics divide on whether O'Neill's three-and-a-half-hour family tragedy remains a masterpiece or an overwrought slog through misery.
